cards.q: Define electric current.
cards.a: The rate of flow of charge: I=ΔQΔt\displaystyle I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}I=ΔtΔQ​.
cards.why: One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.

cards.q: Define the potential difference between two points.
cards.a: The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge moving between the two points: V=WQ\displaystyle V = \frac{W}{Q}V=QW​.
cards.why: Say "per unit charge", not "per coulomb": a definition should not rely on a particular unit.

cards.q: Define the resistance of a component.
cards.a: The ratio of the potential difference across it to the current in it: R=VI\displaystyle R = \frac{V}{I}R=IV​.
cards.why: This definition holds for every component, ohmic or not.

cards.q: State Ohm's law.
cards.a: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (physical conditions) stays constant.
cards.why: The condition earns a mark: without constant temperature the proportionality fails.

cards.q: A student writes: "Ohm's law is R=VI\displaystyle R = \frac{V}{I}R=IV​." What is wrong with this?
cards.a: R=VI\displaystyle R = \frac{V}{I}R=IV​ is the definition of resistance and applies to any component. Ohm's law is the statement that I∝V\displaystyle I \propto VI∝V at constant temperature, which is true only for ohmic conductors.
cards.why: A filament lamp has a resistance VI\displaystyle \frac{V}{I}IV​ at every point on its curve, but it does not obey Ohm's law.

cards.q: Express the volt in terms of the joule and the coulomb.
cards.a: 1 V=1 J C−1\displaystyle 1\ \text{V} = 1\ \text{J C}^{-1}1 V=1 J C−1
cards.why: It follows directly from V=WQ\displaystyle V = \frac{W}{Q}V=QW​.

cards.q: A current of 0.25 A flows for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
cards.a: 30 C
cards.why: The usual slip is leaving the time in minutes.
steps: Convert the time: 2.0 min=120 s\displaystyle 2.0\ \text{min} = 120\ \text{s}2.0 min=120 s.
ΔQ=I Δt=0.25×120\displaystyle \Delta Q = I\,\Delta t = 0.25 \times 120ΔQ=IΔt=0.25×120
ΔQ=30 C\displaystyle \Delta Q = 30\ \text{C}ΔQ=30 C

cards.q: A charge of 30 C passes through a lamp. How many electrons is this? (e=1.60×10−19 C\displaystyle e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}e=1.60×10−19 C)
cards.a: 1.9×1020\displaystyle 1.9 \times 10^{20}1.9×1020 electrons
steps: Each electron carries a charge of magnitude e\displaystyle ee, so N=Qe\displaystyle N = \frac{Q}{e}N=eQ​.
N=301.60×10−19\displaystyle N = \frac{30}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}N=1.60×10−1930​
N=1.9×1020\displaystyle N = 1.9 \times 10^{20}N=1.9×1020

cards.q: 5.0 C of charge passes through a resistor with a potential difference of 12 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred.
cards.a: 60 J
steps: Rearrange V=WQ\displaystyle V = \frac{W}{Q}V=QW​ to W=QV\displaystyle W = QVW=QV.
W=5.0×12\displaystyle W = 5.0 \times 12W=5.0×12
W=60 J\displaystyle W = 60\ \text{J}W=60 J

cards.q: Describe the current–potential difference graph of an ohmic conductor at constant temperature.
cards.a: A straight line through the origin, continuing in the same line for negative values.
cards.afig: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 250" role="img" aria-label="Current against potential difference for an ohmic conductor: a straight line through the origin, continuing in the same way for negative values." class="pg-svg"><rect x="0" y="0" width="360" height="250" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d8d8d8"/><path d="M52 112 L346 112 M195 204 L195 12" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M351 112 l-7 -4 v8 Z M195 7 l-4 7 h8 Z" fill="#1a1a1a"/><text x="195" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">potential difference / V</text><text x="14" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a" transform="rotate(-90 14 112)">current / A</text><text x="187" y="127" text-anchor="end" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">0</text><path d="M63 187.3 L327 36.7" fill="none" stroke="#0b4fa8" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
cards.why: Straight and through the origin together mean I∝V\displaystyle I \propto VI∝V, so the resistance is constant.

cards.q: Describe the shape of the I\displaystyle II–V\displaystyle VV graph of a filament lamp, with I\displaystyle II on the vertical axis.
cards.a: A curve through the origin whose gradient decreases as V\displaystyle VV increases, in both directions (an S-shape through the origin).
cards.afig: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 250" role="img" aria-label="Current against potential difference for a filament lamp: a curve through the origin that gets less steep as the potential difference increases, in both directions." class="pg-svg"><rect x="0" y="0" width="360" height="250" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d8d8d8"/><path d="M52 112 L346 112 M195 204 L195 12" fill="none" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M351 112 l-7 -4 v8 Z M195 7 l-4 7 h8 Z" fill="#1a1a1a"/><text x="195" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">potential difference / V</text><text x="14" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a" transform="rotate(-90 14 112)">current / A</text><text x="187" y="127" text-anchor="end" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#1a1a1a">0</text><path d="M63 192 L68.5 190 L74 187.9 L79.5 185.9 L85 183.7 L90.5 181.5 L96 179.3 L101.5 177.1 L107 174.7 L112.5 172.3 L118 169.9 L123.5 167.4 L129 164.8 L134.5 162.1 L140 159.3 L145.5 156.4 L151 153.4 L156.5 150.2 L162 146.8 L167.5 143.2 L173 139.3 L178.5 135 L184 130 L189.5 123.9 L195 112 L200.5 100.1 L206 94 L211.5 89 L217 84.7 L222.5 80.8 L228 77.2 L233.5 73.8 L239 70.6 L244.5 67.6 L250 64.7 L255.5 61.9 L261 59.2 L266.5 56.6 L272 54.1 L277.5 51.7 L283 49.3 L288.5 47 L294 44.7 L299.5 42.5 L305 40.3 L310.5 38.2 L316 36.1 L321.5 34 L327 32" fill="none" stroke="#0b4fa8" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>
cards.why: The curve flattens because the resistance rises as the filament heats up.

cards.q: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current in it increases.
cards.a: A larger current heats the filament, and a hotter metal has a higher resistance.
marks: The current transfers energy to the filament, so its temperature rises.
The lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude.
Conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently.
So a larger potential difference is needed for each unit of current: the resistance increases.

cards.q: Describe the I\displaystyle II–V\displaystyle VV characteristic of a semiconductor diode.
cards.a: In the forward direction almost no current flows until a threshold of about 0.6 V (silicon), then the current rises steeply. In the reverse direction the current is almost zero.
cards.why: The diode has a very high resistance in reverse and a low resistance once it conducts in the forward direction.

cards.q: A student finds the resistance of a filament lamp from the gradient of a tangent to its I\displaystyle II–V\displaystyle VV curve. Why is this wrong?
cards.a: Resistance is defined as VI\displaystyle \frac{V}{I}IV​ at that point: read the two values and divide. The gradient only gives the resistance when the graph is a straight line through the origin.
cards.why: For a curve, the tangent's gradient is ΔIΔV\displaystyle \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta V}ΔVΔI​, which is not IV\displaystyle \frac{I}{V}VI​.

cards.q: What resistance does an ideal ammeter have, and an ideal voltmeter?
cards.a: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
cards.why: Then the ammeter takes no potential difference and the voltmeter takes no current, so neither changes the circuit it measures.

cards.q: A filament lamp's characteristic is drawn with V\displaystyle VV on the vertical axis and I\displaystyle II on the horizontal axis. How does the curve bend?
cards.a: It curves upwards: the gradient increases as I\displaystyle II increases.
cards.why: Swapping the axes flips the curve. Check which quantity is on which axis before describing a characteristic.

cards.q: Describe the I\displaystyle II–V\displaystyle VV graph of an NTC thermistor as the current heats it, with I\displaystyle II on the vertical axis.
cards.a: A curve through the origin whose gradient increases as V\displaystyle VV increases.
cards.why: As the thermistor warms, its resistance falls, so each extra volt drives more extra current. It is the opposite of a filament lamp.

cards.q: Define the resistivity of a material, giving the equation.
cards.a: ρ=RAL\displaystyle \rho = \frac{RA}{L}ρ=LRA​, where R\displaystyle RR is the resistance of a sample of length L\displaystyle LL and cross-sectional area A\displaystyle AA. It is a property of the material (at a given temperature), not of the particular wire.

cards.q: State the SI unit of resistivity.
cards.a: The ohm metre, Ω m\displaystyle \Omega\ \text{m}Ω m.
cards.why: It is ohm times metre, not ohm per metre: RAL\displaystyle \frac{RA}{L}LRA​ has units Ω m2m\displaystyle \frac{\Omega\ \text{m}^{2}}{\text{m}}mΩ m2​.

cards.q: A copper wire is 2.0 m long with a diameter of 0.50 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7×10−8 Ω m\displaystyle 1.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\ \text{m}1.7×10−8 Ω m. Calculate its resistance.
cards.a: 0.17 Ω
cards.why: Two common slips: using the diameter as the radius, and leaving millimetres unconverted.
steps: Radius: r=0.25 mm=0.25×10−3 m\displaystyle r = 0.25\ \text{mm} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}r=0.25 mm=0.25×10−3 m.
Area: A=πr2=π(0.25×10−3)2=1.96×10−7 m2\displaystyle A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (0.25 \times 10^{-3})^{2} = 1.96 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}A=πr2=π(0.25×10−3)2=1.96×10−7 m2.
R=ρLA=1.7×10−8×2.01.96×10−7\displaystyle R = \frac{\rho L}{A} = \frac{1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 2.0}{1.96 \times 10^{-7}}R=AρL​=1.96×10−71.7×10−8×2.0​
R=0.17 Ω\displaystyle R = 0.17\ \OmegaR=0.17 Ω

cards.q: A wire has a diameter of 0.40 mm. Calculate its cross-sectional area in m2\displaystyle \text{m}^{2}m2.
cards.a: 1.3×10−7 m2\displaystyle 1.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}1.3×10−7 m2
cards.why: Halve the diameter first, and convert to metres before squaring.
steps: Radius: r=0.20 mm=0.20×10−3 m\displaystyle r = 0.20\ \text{mm} = 0.20 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}r=0.20 mm=0.20×10−3 m.
A=πr2=π(0.20×10−3)2\displaystyle A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (0.20 \times 10^{-3})^{2}A=πr2=π(0.20×10−3)2
A=1.3×10−7 m2\displaystyle A = 1.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}A=1.3×10−7 m2

cards.q: A wire is replaced by one of the same material with twice the length and twice the diameter. How does the resistance change?
cards.a: It halves.
cards.why: Area depends on the square of the diameter.
steps: R=ρLA\displaystyle R = \frac{\rho L}{A}R=AρL​, so doubling L\displaystyle LL doubles R\displaystyle RR.
Doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, which divides R\displaystyle RR by 4.
Overall: R×2÷4=R2\displaystyle R \times 2 \div 4 = \frac{R}{2}R×2÷4=2R​.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the resistivity of a metal wire.
cards.a: Find the resistance of several different lengths, plot R\displaystyle RR against L\displaystyle LL, and use the gradient with the cross-sectional area.
marks: Measure the diameter with a micrometer at several places and orientations, and take the mean.
Calculate the area from A=πd24\displaystyle A = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}A=4πd2​.
For each length L\displaystyle LL, measure V\displaystyle VV and I\displaystyle II and calculate R=VI\displaystyle R = \frac{V}{I}R=IV​.
Plot R\displaystyle RR against L\displaystyle LL: a straight line with gradient ρA\displaystyle \frac{\rho}{A}Aρ​.
ρ=gradient×A\displaystyle \rho = \text{gradient} \times Aρ=gradient×A.

cards.q: In the resistivity experiment, why is the current kept small and switched off between readings?
cards.a: To stop the wire heating up. A rise in temperature would increase its resistance, so the readings would not all be for the same resistivity.

cards.q: In the resistivity experiment, which measurement usually contributes most to the uncertainty in ρ\displaystyle \rhoρ, and why?
cards.a: The diameter. It is very small, so its percentage uncertainty is large, and because A∝d2\displaystyle A \propto d^{2}A∝d2 that percentage uncertainty is doubled.

cards.q: A wire's diameter is measured as 0.38±0.01 mm\displaystyle 0.38 \pm 0.01\ \text{mm}0.38±0.01 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in its cross-sectional area.
cards.a: 5.3%
cards.why: When a quantity is raised to a power, multiply its percentage uncertainty by that power.
steps: Percentage uncertainty in d\displaystyle dd: 0.010.38×100=2.6%\displaystyle \frac{0.01}{0.38} \times 100 = 2.6\%0.380.01​×100=2.6%.
A∝d2\displaystyle A \propto d^{2}A∝d2, so the percentage uncertainty doubles.
2×2.6%=5.3%\displaystyle 2 \times 2.6\% = 5.3\%2×2.6%=5.3%

cards.q: A graph of R\displaystyle RR against L\displaystyle LL for a wire is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. Suggest a cause, and state whether it affects the value of ρ\displaystyle \rhoρ.
cards.a: A systematic error, such as contact resistance at the clips or a zero error in the length. It shifts every point by the same amount, so the gradient, and therefore ρ\displaystyle \rhoρ, is unaffected.
cards.why: This is why the gradient is used, not a single pair of readings.

cards.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal conductor increases when its temperature rises.
cards.a: The lattice ions vibrate more, so conduction electrons collide with them more often.
marks: The positive ions of the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude at a higher temperature.
Conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently.
The number of conduction electrons stays about the same, so the current for a given potential difference falls: resistance increases.

cards.q: How does the resistance of an NTC thermistor change as its temperature rises, and why?
cards.a: Its resistance decreases.
cards.why: NTC stands for negative temperature coefficient.
marks: Heating gives electrons enough energy to break free, so the number of conduction electrons increases greatly.
The lattice vibrations also increase, which on its own would raise the resistance.
The increase in the number of charge carriers has the larger effect, so the resistance falls.

aqa.note: AQA asks for the qualitative effect; the explanation is useful support.

cards.q: Describe the resistance–temperature graph of an NTC thermistor.
cards.a: A curve that falls as temperature rises: steep at low temperatures and levelling off at high temperatures. It is not a straight line.

cards.q: What is a superconductor?
cards.a: A material that has zero resistivity at and below a critical temperature.
cards.why: The critical temperature depends on the material.

cards.q: Give two applications of superconductors.
cards.a: Producing strong magnetic fields (very large currents with no heating), and reducing energy loss in the transmission of electric power.

cards.q: In I=nqvA\displaystyle I = nqvAI=nqvA, what does each symbol stand for?
cards.a: I\displaystyle II: current. n\displaystyle nn: number of charge carriers per unit volume. q\displaystyle qq: charge on each carrier. v\displaystyle vv: drift velocity of the carriers. A\displaystyle AA: cross-sectional area of the conductor.
cards.why: n\displaystyle nn is a number density, with unit m−3\displaystyle \text{m}^{-3}m−3: it is not the total number of carriers.

cards.q: Use I=nqvA\displaystyle I = nqvAI=nqvA to explain why metals, semiconductors and insulators have such different resistivities.
cards.a: They differ enormously in n\displaystyle nn, the number of charge carriers per unit volume.
marks: Metals have a very large n\displaystyle nn (about one or more free electrons per atom), so a large current flows for a given drift velocity: low resistivity.
Semiconductors have a much smaller n\displaystyle nn, so their resistivity is much higher.
Insulators have almost no free charge carriers, so n\displaystyle nn is negligible and the resistivity is extremely high.

cards.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0×10−6 m2\displaystyle 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2}1.0×10−6 m2 carries a current of 2.0 A. Copper has 8.5×1028\displaystyle 8.5 \times 10^{28}8.5×1028 free electrons per m3\displaystyle \text{m}^{3}m3. Calculate the drift velocity. (e=1.60×10−19 C\displaystyle e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}e=1.60×10−19 C)
cards.a: 1.5×10−4 m s−1\displaystyle 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}1.5×10−4 m s−1
cards.why: Drift velocities are tiny, a fraction of a millimetre per second, even for large currents.
steps: Rearrange I=nqvA\displaystyle I = nqvAI=nqvA to v=InqA\displaystyle v = \frac{I}{nqA}v=nqAI​.
v=2.08.5×1028×1.60×10−19×1.0×10−6\displaystyle v = \frac{2.0}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}}v=8.5×1028×1.60×10−19×1.0×10−62.0​
v=1.5×10−4 m s−1\displaystyle v = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}v=1.5×10−4 m s−1

cards.q: How does the resistance of a light dependent resistor (LDR) change as the light intensity on it increases?
cards.a: Its resistance decreases.
cards.why: Light releases more conduction electrons in the semiconductor, so there are more charge carriers.

cards.q: The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it. Which conservation law is this a consequence of?
cards.a: Conservation of charge.
cards.why: Charge cannot build up or disappear at a junction, so what flows in each second must flow out.

cards.q: Around any closed loop of a circuit, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences. Which conservation law is this a consequence of?
cards.a: Conservation of energy.
cards.why: The energy given to each unit of charge by the sources equals the energy it transfers in the components round the loop.

cards.q: State the equations for the total resistance of resistors in series, and in parallel.
cards.a: Series: RT=R1+R2+R3+…\displaystyle R_{T} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3} + \dotsRT​=R1​+R2​+R3​+… Parallel: 1RT=1R1+1R2+1R3+…\displaystyle \frac{1}{R_{T}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}} + \frac{1}{R_{3}} + \dotsRT​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​+R3​1​+…

edexcel.note: Not on the Edexcel formulae sheet: you must know these and be able to derive them.

cards.q: Derive the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in series.
cards.a: RT=R1+R2\displaystyle R_{T} = R_{1} + R_{2}RT​=R1​+R2​
steps: Conservation of charge: the same current I\displaystyle II is in both resistors.
Conservation of energy: the total potential difference is the sum, V=V1+V2\displaystyle V = V_{1} + V_{2}V=V1​+V2​.
Use V=IR\displaystyle V = IRV=IR for each: IRT=IR1+IR2\displaystyle IR_{T} = IR_{1} + IR_{2}IRT​=IR1​+IR2​.
Divide by I\displaystyle II: RT=R1+R2\displaystyle R_{T} = R_{1} + R_{2}RT​=R1​+R2​.

cards.q: Derive the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in parallel.
cards.a: 1RT=1R1+1R2\displaystyle \frac{1}{R_{T}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}}RT​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​
steps: Conservation of energy: the potential difference V\displaystyle VV is the same across both resistors.
Conservation of charge: the total current is the sum, I=I1+I2\displaystyle I = I_{1} + I_{2}I=I1​+I2​.
Use I=VR\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​ for each: VRT=VR1+VR2\displaystyle \frac{V}{R_{T}} = \frac{V}{R_{1}} + \frac{V}{R_{2}}RT​V​=R1​V​+R2​V​.
Divide by V\displaystyle VV: 1RT=1R1+1R2\displaystyle \frac{1}{R_{T}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}}RT​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​.

cards.q: Calculate the total resistance of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor connected in parallel.
cards.a: 2.0 Ω
cards.why: The usual slip is forgetting the final reciprocal and giving 0.50 Ω.
steps: 1RT=16.0+13.0=16.0+26.0=36.0\displaystyle \frac{1}{R_{T}} = \frac{1}{6.0} + \frac{1}{3.0} = \frac{1}{6.0} + \frac{2}{6.0} = \frac{3}{6.0}RT​1​=6.01​+3.01​=6.01​+6.02​=6.03​
Take the reciprocal: RT=6.03=2.0 Ω\displaystyle R_{T} = \frac{6.0}{3} = 2.0\ \OmegaRT​=36.0​=2.0 Ω

cards.q: How does the total resistance of resistors in parallel compare with the smallest individual resistance?
cards.a: It is always less than the smallest one.
cards.why: Each added branch is an extra route for charge, so more current flows for the same potential difference. Use this to check a calculated answer.

cards.q: A 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. Calculate the potential difference across the parallel pair.
cards.a: 4.0 V
cards.why: Check: the 4.0 Ω resistor takes 8.0 V, and 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 V.
steps: Parallel pair: 1R=16.0+13.0\displaystyle \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{6.0} + \frac{1}{3.0}R1​=6.01​+3.01​, so R=2.0 Ω\displaystyle R = 2.0\ \OmegaR=2.0 Ω.
Total resistance: 4.0+2.0=6.0 Ω\displaystyle 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0\ \Omega4.0+2.0=6.0 Ω.
Current from the supply: I=126.0=2.0 A\displaystyle I = \frac{12}{6.0} = 2.0\ \text{A}I=6.012​=2.0 A.
Potential difference across the pair: V=IR=2.0×2.0=4.0 V\displaystyle V = IR = 2.0 \times 2.0 = 4.0\ \text{V}V=IR=2.0×2.0=4.0 V.

cards.q: Two different resistors are connected in series. Which form of the power equation shows most directly which one dissipates more power: P=I2R\displaystyle P = I^{2}RP=I2R or P=V2R\displaystyle P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}P=RV2​?
cards.a: P=I2R\displaystyle P = I^{2}RP=I2R. In series the current is the same in both, so the larger resistance dissipates more power.
cards.why: In parallel the potential difference is the same, so use P=V2R\displaystyle P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}P=RV2​: there the smaller resistance dissipates more.

cards.q: Starting from P=VI\displaystyle P = VIP=VI, derive P=I2R\displaystyle P = I^{2}RP=I2R and P=V2R\displaystyle P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}P=RV2​.
cards.a: Substitute V=IR\displaystyle V = IRV=IR, then I=VR\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​.
steps: Substitute V=IR\displaystyle V = IRV=IR into P=VI\displaystyle P = VIP=VI: P=(IR)I=I2R\displaystyle P = (IR)I = I^{2}RP=(IR)I=I2R.
Substitute I=VR\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​ into P=VI\displaystyle P = VIP=VI: P=V×VR=V2R\displaystyle P = V \times \frac{V}{R} = \frac{V^{2}}{R}P=V×RV​=RV2​.

cards.q: A heater takes a current of 8.7 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate the energy it transfers in 3.0 minutes.
cards.a: 3.6×105 J\displaystyle 3.6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}3.6×105 J
steps: Convert the time: 3.0 min=180 s\displaystyle 3.0\ \text{min} = 180\ \text{s}3.0 min=180 s.

cards.q: A student says: "Current gets used up as it goes through a lamp." Correct this.
cards.a: The current is the same on both sides of the lamp, because charge is conserved. What the lamp takes from the charge is energy: each unit of charge leaves with less electrical potential energy.

cards.q: Three cells, each of emf 1.5 V, are connected in series in the same direction. What is the total emf, and what happens to the internal resistance?
cards.a: The total emf is 4.5 V: emfs in series add. The internal resistances also add.

cards.q: Two identical cells, each of emf ε\displaystyle \varepsilonε and internal resistance r\displaystyle rr, are connected in parallel. State the emf and the internal resistance of the combination.
cards.a: The emf is still ε\displaystyle \varepsilonε. The internal resistance is r2\displaystyle \frac{r}{2}2r​.
cards.why: Each cell supplies half the current, so the combination lasts longer and loses fewer volts, but it does not push any harder.

cards.q: A student says: "In a parallel circuit the current takes the path of least resistance." Correct this.
cards.a: Every branch carries current. The current divides so that the branch with the smaller resistance carries the larger share: the currents are in the inverse ratio of the resistances.
cards.why: The potential difference is the same across each branch, so I=VR\displaystyle I = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​ in every one.

cards.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series across a supply. Compared with one lamp alone across the same supply, what power does each lamp now dissipate? Assume the resistance of a lamp stays constant.
cards.a: One quarter of the power.
steps: Each lamp now has half the supply potential difference across it.
P=V2R\displaystyle P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}P=RV2​, so halving V\displaystyle VV gives (12)2=14\displaystyle \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}(21​)2=41​ of the power.

cards.q: What is a potential divider?
cards.a: Two or more resistors in series across a supply, which share the supply potential difference in proportion to their resistances.
cards.why: The same current is in each, and V=IR\displaystyle V = IRV=IR, so the larger resistance takes the larger share.

cards.q: Resistors R1\displaystyle R_{1}R1​ and R2\displaystyle R_{2}R2​ are in series across a supply Vin\displaystyle V_{\text{in}}Vin​. Write the equation for the potential difference across R2\displaystyle R_{2}R2​.
cards.a: Vout=Vin×R2R1+R2\displaystyle V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}Vout​=Vin​×R1​+R2​R2​​
cards.why: The resistor you are finding the potential difference across goes on top.

cards.q: A 4.0 kΩ resistor and a 2.0 kΩ resistor are in series across a 12 V supply. Calculate the potential difference across the 2.0 kΩ resistor.
cards.a: 4.0 V
cards.why: Both resistances are in kilohms, so the ratio needs no conversion.
steps: Vout=Vin×R2R1+R2\displaystyle V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}Vout​=Vin​×R1​+R2​R2​​

cards.q: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply. Explain what happens to the potential difference across the fixed resistor when the temperature rises.
cards.a: It increases.
cards.why: Alternatively: the total resistance falls, the current rises, and V=IR\displaystyle V = IRV=IR for the fixed resistor rises.
marks: The resistance of the thermistor decreases as the temperature rises.
The thermistor now takes a smaller share of the supply potential difference.
The supply potential difference is unchanged, so the potential difference across the fixed resistor increases.

cards.q: An LDR and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply. A lamp must switch on when it gets dark. Across which component should the switching circuit be connected, and why?
cards.a: Across the LDR.
marks: In the dark the resistance of the LDR increases.
The LDR takes a larger share of the supply potential difference.
The rising potential difference across the LDR can be used to switch the lamp on.

cards.q: Two 10 kΩ resistors are in series across a 12 V supply. A load of resistance 10 kΩ is then connected across one of them. Calculate the potential difference across the load.
cards.a: 4.0 V
cards.why: Without the load the output would be 6.0 V. Connecting a load lowers the output of a potential divider.
steps: The load is in parallel with one 10 kΩ resistor: 1R=110+110\displaystyle \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}R1​=101​+101​, so R=5.0 kΩ\displaystyle R = 5.0\ \text{k}\OmegaR=5.0 kΩ.
The divider is now 10 kΩ in series with 5.0 kΩ.
V=12×5.010+5.0=4.0 V\displaystyle V = 12 \times \frac{5.0}{10 + 5.0} = 4.0\ \text{V}V=12×10+5.05.0​=4.0 V

cards.q: A uniform wire carries a steady current. How does the potential difference across a section of the wire depend on the length of that section?
cards.a: It is directly proportional to the length.
cards.why: For a uniform wire, resistance is proportional to length, and the current is the same throughout, so V=IR∝L\displaystyle V = IR \propto LV=IR∝L.

cards.q: A variable resistor is connected as a potential divider across a supply (three terminals used, output taken from the sliding contact). What range of output potential difference can it give?
cards.a: From zero up to the full supply potential difference.
cards.why: A variable resistor simply placed in series with a component cannot reduce the potential difference across it to zero.

cards.q: Define the electromotive force (emf) of a source.
cards.a: The energy transferred to electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source: ε=EQ\displaystyle \varepsilon = \frac{E}{Q}ε=QE​.
cards.why: It is energy per unit charge, measured in volts. It is not a force.

cards.q: What is meant by the internal resistance of a cell?
cards.a: The resistance of the cell itself to the current passing through it. Some of the energy given to each unit of charge is dissipated inside the cell.

cards.q: What is the terminal potential difference of a cell?
cards.a: The potential difference across the terminals of the cell: the energy per unit charge delivered to the external circuit. V=ε−Ir\displaystyle V = \varepsilon - IrV=ε−Ir.

cards.q: In ε=I(R+r)\displaystyle \varepsilon = I(R + r)ε=I(R+r), what do the terms IR\displaystyle IRIR and Ir\displaystyle IrIr represent?
cards.a: IR\displaystyle IRIR is the terminal potential difference, across the external resistance R\displaystyle RR. Ir\displaystyle IrIr is the potential difference across the internal resistance r\displaystyle rr, often called the lost volts.

edexcel.note: Not on the Edexcel formulae sheet.

cards.q: When is the terminal potential difference of a cell equal to its emf?
cards.a: Only when there is no current in the cell (open circuit). Whenever a current flows, the terminal potential difference is less than the emf by Ir\displaystyle IrIr.
cards.why: Examiners report that using the emf as the terminal potential difference is one of the most common errors in circuit questions.

cards.q: A cell of emf 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω resistor. Calculate the terminal potential difference.
cards.a: 5.5 V

steps: Current: I=εR+r=6.05.5+0.50=1.0 A\displaystyle I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r} = \frac{6.0}{5.5 + 0.50} = 1.0\ \text{A}I=R+rε​=5.5+0.506.0​=1.0 A.
Terminal potential difference: V=IR=1.0×5.5\displaystyle V = IR = 1.0 \times 5.5V=IR=1.0×5.5
V=5.5 V\displaystyle V = 5.5\ \text{V}V=5.5 V

cards.q: Outline how to determine the emf and internal resistance of a cell.
cards.a: Measure the terminal potential difference for a range of currents and plot V\displaystyle VV against I\displaystyle II.
marks: Connect the cell to a variable resistor, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the cell's terminals.
Change the resistance to obtain a range of values of current I\displaystyle II and terminal potential difference V\displaystyle VV.
Plot V\displaystyle VV (vertical axis) against I\displaystyle II.
V=ε−Ir\displaystyle V = \varepsilon - IrV=ε−Ir, so the graph is a straight line: the intercept on the V\displaystyle VV axis is ε\displaystyle \varepsilonε.
The gradient is −r\displaystyle -r−r.

cards.q: For a cell, a graph of terminal potential difference V\displaystyle VV against current I\displaystyle II is plotted. What do the intercept on the V\displaystyle VV axis and the gradient represent?
cards.a: The intercept is the emf. The gradient is −r\displaystyle -r−r: its magnitude is the internal resistance.

cards.q: In the internal resistance experiment, why is the switch opened between readings and large currents avoided?
cards.a: So that the cell does not run down or heat up during the experiment, either of which would change its emf and internal resistance.

cards.q: Explain why a car's headlamps dim when the starter motor is switched on.
cards.a: The battery's terminal potential difference falls because of its internal resistance.
marks: The starter motor draws a very large current from the battery.
The potential difference across the internal resistance (lost volts, Ir\displaystyle IrIr) becomes large.
The terminal potential difference V=ε−Ir\displaystyle V = \varepsilon - IrV=ε−Ir falls.
The headlamps are connected across the terminals, so they have a smaller potential difference and dissipate less power.

cards.q: A cell of emf ε\displaystyle \varepsilonε and internal resistance r\displaystyle rr is short-circuited by a wire of negligible resistance. What is the current?
cards.a: I=εr\displaystyle I = \frac{\varepsilon}{r}I=rε​. This is the maximum current the cell can supply.
cards.why: With R=0\displaystyle R = 0R=0, ε=I(R+r)\displaystyle \varepsilon = I(R + r)ε=I(R+r) becomes ε=Ir\displaystyle \varepsilon = Irε=Ir. All the energy is dissipated inside the cell.

cards.q: Multiply ε=IR+Ir\displaystyle \varepsilon = IR + Irε=IR+Ir through by I\displaystyle II. What does each term of the result represent?
cards.a: εI=I2R+I2r\displaystyle \varepsilon I = I^{2}R + I^{2}rεI=I2R+I2r. εI\displaystyle \varepsilon IεI is the total power supplied by the cell, I2R\displaystyle I^{2}RI2R is the power delivered to the external resistance, and I2r\displaystyle I^{2}rI2r is the power wasted inside the cell.

cards.q: Why does a high-resistance voltmeter connected directly across a cell read a value very close to the cell's emf?
cards.a: The voltmeter draws a negligible current, so the lost volts Ir\displaystyle IrIr are negligible and the terminal potential difference is almost equal to the emf.
